replacement: “‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant. That is what You turned down, for the sake of the freedom You placed above everything else. Yet the great secret of this world lies hidden in that question. Had You chosen “bread,” You would have satisfied the universal and everlasting craving of all humanity—the craving to find someone to worship. A man who is free has no goal he pursues so restlessly and so painfully as this: to find someone to worship. But he wants to worship something no one can dispute, something so plainly established that all men would agree at once to bow to it. These pitiful creatures are not satisfied to find what this man or that man can worship. They must find something that everyone will believe in and worship, and above all they must do it _together_. This craving for worship in _common_ has been the chief misery of each man, and of the whole race, since time began. For the sake of common worship they have put each other to the sword. They have set up gods and challenged one another: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods!” So it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have vanished from the earth. They will fall down before idols all the same. You knew this basic secret of human nature. You could not help knowing it. Yet You refused the one sure banner that was held out to You, the banner that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread. You refused it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Now see what You did next. And again, all of it in the name of freedom! I tell You, no anxiety torments man more than the need to find, and quickly, someone to whom he can hand over the gift of freedom with which the poor creature is born. But only one who can quiet their conscience can take their freedom from them. In bread You were offered a banner nothing could beat: give men bread and they will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gets hold of man’s conscience—oh! then he will throw away Your bread and follow the one who has trapped his conscience. In that You were right. The secret of man’s existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man would not agree to go on living. He would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even with bread in plenty. That is true. But what came of it? Instead of taking men’s freedom away, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man prefers peace, even death, to the freedom of choosing in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing tempts man more than his freedom of conscience, and nothing makes him suffer more. And now see: instead of building a firm foundation to put man’s conscience at rest for ever, You chose everything that is exceptional, vague and puzzling. You chose what was wholly beyond men’s strength, and acted as though You did not love them at all—You, who came to give Your life for them! Instead of taking over men’s freedom, You added to it. You loaded the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings for ever. You wanted man’s love given freely. You wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and made captive by You. In place of the rigid ancient law, man would now have to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But did You not know that in the end he would reject even Your image and Your truth, once the fearful burden of free choice weighed him down? In the end they will cry out that the truth is not in You. They could not have been left in worse confusion and torment than You have left them in, piling on them so many cares and so many problems that have no answer.

“‘When they receive bread from us, they will see plainly that we take the bread their own hands have made, only to hand it back to them, and that there is no miracle in it. They will see that we do not turn stones into bread. Yet in truth they will be more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! They will remember only too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they came back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. Too, too well will they understand the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame that they do not? Speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures, which is what they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them in the end not to be proud, because You lifted them up and so taught them pride. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children, and that a child’s happiness is the sweetest there is. They will grow timid. They will look to us and press close to us in fear, as chicks do to the hen. They will marvel at us and stand in awe of us. They will take pride in our being so powerful and so clever that we could tame a flock this unruly, thousands of millions strong. They will tremble helplessly when we are angry, their minds will fill with fear, and they will cry as easily as women and children do. But at a sign from us they will turn just as readily to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their free hours we shall arrange their life like a child’s game, with children’s songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall even let them sin. They are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we let them sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for if it is done with our permission. We let them sin because we love them, we shall say, and the punishment for these sins we take on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as the saviors who have borne their sins before God. They will keep no secrets from us. We shall permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, and to have children or not, depending on whether they have obeyed or disobeyed, and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience, all, all of them, they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for all. They will be glad to believe our answer, for it will spare them the great anxiety and the terrible agony they suffer now, having to decide freely for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken on themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall tempt them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for such as they. It is prophesied that You will come again in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and the strong. But we will say that they have saved only themselves, and we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the _mystery_ in her hands, will be put to shame; that the weak will rise up again, tear her royal purple, and strip her loathsome body bare. But then I will stand up and show You the thousand millions of happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins on ourselves for their happiness, will stand before You and say: “Judge us, if You can and dare.” Know that I do not fear You. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom You have blessed men with, and that I too was struggling to take my place among Your elect, among the strong and mighty, hungering “to make up the number.” But I woke up, and I refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Your work_. I left the proud and returned to the humble, for the humble’s happiness. What I tell You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I repeat, tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, which at one sign from me will rush to pile the glowing coals around the stake where I shall burn You for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I shall burn You. _Dixi._’”

“So what if it is! You’ve finally guessed it. It’s perfectly true, that is the whole secret. But isn’t that suffering, at least for a man like him, who has thrown away his whole life in the desert and still could not shake off his incurable love for humanity? In his old age he arrived at a clear conviction: only the advice of the great, dread spirit could make any tolerable life for those feeble, unruly ‘incomplete, experimental creatures made as a joke.’ Convinced of this, he sees that he has to follow the counsel of the wise spirit, the dread spirit of death and destruction. So he has to accept lies and deception, and lead men knowingly to death and destruction, while deceiving them the whole way so that they never notice where they are being taken. That way the poor blind creatures can at least believe themselves happy on the road. And mark this: the deception is carried out in the name of Him Whose ideal the old man believed in so fervently all his life. Isn’t that tragic? And if just one such man stood at the head of the whole army ‘filled with the lust for power only for the sake of filthy gain,’ wouldn’t one be enough to make a tragedy? More than that, one such man at the head is enough to produce the true guiding idea of the Roman Church, with all its armies and Jesuits, its highest idea. I tell you frankly, I firmly believe there has always been a man like that among those at the head of the movement. Who knows, there may have been some even among the Roman Popes. Who knows, perhaps the spirit of that accursed old man, who loves mankind so obstinately in his own fashion, lives on right now in a whole crowd of such old men. They would exist not by chance but by agreement, as a secret league formed long ago to guard the mystery, to guard it from the weak and unhappy, in order to make them happy. No doubt that’s how it is, and how it has to be. I suspect even the Masons have something of the same mystery at bottom, and that’s why the Catholics hate the Masons so, as rivals who break up the unity of the idea, when it is so essential that there be one flock and one shepherd.... But the way I’m defending my idea, I might be an author who can’t take your criticism. Enough of that.”

“This is how I meant to end it. When the Inquisitor finished speaking, he waited a while for his Prisoner to answer. The silence was heavy on him. He had seen that the Prisoner listened closely the whole time, gazing gently into his face, and clearly did not want to reply. The old man longed for Him to say something, however bitter and terrible. But He suddenly came up to the old man without a word and kissed him softly on his bloodless, aged lips. That was His whole answer. The old man shuddered. His lips moved. He went to the door, opened it, and said to Him: ‘Go, and come no more... do not come at all, never, never!’ And he let Him out into the dark alleys of the town. The Prisoner went away.”

“Oh, it’s all nonsense, Alyosha. It’s just a senseless poem by a senseless student who never managed to write two lines of verse. Why take it so seriously? You can’t think I’m about to run off to the Jesuits and join the men who are correcting His work? Good Lord, that’s none of my business. I told you, all I want is to live on until thirty, and then... dash the cup to the ground!”
